title: What Made Being 10 Years Old in 1963 So Special?

scenes.text: Ten years old. For many people, it's the best age there is. Old enough to ride your bike across town, but too young to have any real worries. Old enough to stay up for a TV show, but young enough to still believe the world was mostly good. And if you were ten years old in nineteen sixty-three, you had one of the best years of all.
scenes.caption: TEN YEARS OLD

scenes.text: If you were ten in sixty-three, you were born in nineteen fifty-three, right in the heart of the baby boom. You grew up surrounded by kids. Your classroom had thirty-five children in it. Your street had dozens. Wherever you went, there was always somebody to play with.
scenes.caption: BORN IN 1953

scenes.text: So today, let's look at ten things that made being ten years old in nineteen sixty-three so special. Ten, for ten years old. See how many of them were true for you.
scenes.caption: TEN REASONS

scenes.text: The first reason was freedom. A ten-year-old in nineteen sixty-three could leave the house after breakfast and not come back until lunch, or dinner. Mothers didn't ask exactly where you were going. They just said, be home when the streetlights come on. And you were.
scenes.caption: BE HOME BY THE STREETLIGHTS

scenes.text: Kids roamed in packs. They rode bikes to the creek, the woods, the vacant lot and the five-and-dime. They built forts out of scrap lumber and climbed trees that were much too high. If somebody got hurt, they walked home bleeding, got a Band-Aid and some Mercurochrome, and went right back out.
scenes.caption: FORTS AND CREEKS

scenes.text: Ten-year-olds also walked to school, often a mile or more, without a grown-up. They crossed busy streets with a crossing guard, or a sixth grader in a white safety patrol belt. Along the way, they collected friends, kicked rocks, and stopped to look at anything interesting.
scenes.query: 1960s children walking to school crossing guard
scenes.caption: WALKING TO SCHOOL

scenes.text: And ten-year-olds had a lot of responsibility. They watched their little brothers and sisters. They walked to the corner store with a note from their mother and a few dollars, and came back with milk, bread and the right change. They took out the trash, fed the dog and mowed the lawn. Nobody thought of a ten-year-old as a little kid.
scenes.caption: REAL RESPONSIBILITY

scenes.text: The second reason was outer space. For a ten-year-old in nineteen sixty-three, astronauts were the greatest heroes in the world. John Glenn had orbited the Earth in February of nineteen sixty-two. In May of sixty-three, Gordon Cooper flew for more than a day in Faith Seven, the last flight of Project Mercury.
scenes.caption: GORDON COOPER, MAY 1963

scenes.text: Schools wheeled televisions into classrooms so children could watch the launches live. Teachers counted down with the announcer. And every child dreamed of going to the moon, because President Kennedy had promised that Americans would land there before the end of the decade. A ten-year-old in sixty-three would be sixteen when it happened.
scenes.caption: WATCHING THE LAUNCH

scenes.text: Kids drank Tang, because astronauts did. They built model rockets. They collected astronaut trading cards, and wore space helmets made from cardboard boxes. Many of the scientists and engineers of the next generation said they got their start at ten, watching those rockets on a school TV.
scenes.caption: TANG AND MODEL ROCKETS

scenes.text: The third reason was television. In nineteen sixty-three, more than nine in ten American homes had a TV, and kids had some of the best shows ever made. The Andy Griffith Show. The Dick Van Dyke Show. The Beverly Hillbillies, which was the most popular show in America. And Leave It to Beaver, in its final season.
scenes.caption: THE BEVERLY HILLBILLIES

scenes.text: There was The Flintstones and The Jetsons in prime time. Lassie and Walt Disney on Sunday nights. Bonanza, Gunsmoke and The Fugitive, which started that fall. And on Saturday mornings, Bugs Bunny, Mighty Mouse and Sky King. Almost all of it was still in black and white.
scenes.caption: SATURDAY MORNING

scenes.text: Ten-year-olds also had local kids' shows, with a host in a costume, a studio audience of children, and cartoons in between. Every city had one, with a clown, a cowboy or a sea captain. Kids waited months for a chance to be in the audience, and wore their best clothes when they finally went.
scenes.caption: THE LOCAL KIDS' SHOW

scenes.text: And there was the radio. At night, ten-year-olds hid transistor radios under their pillows, listening to ball games and rock and roll stations long after lights out. On summer evenings, the sound of a baseball game drifted from every porch. Many people still associate the voice of their team's announcer with being ten years old.
scenes.caption: UNDER THE PILLOW

scenes.text: The fourth reason was the toys. In nineteen sixty-three, kids had Barbie, Ken and Skipper, the Easy-Bake Oven which came out that year, and the Hula Hoop. Boys had cap guns, Matchbox cars, Erector sets and electric trains. There were Slinkys, yo-yos, kites, marbles and jacks.
scenes.caption: THE EASY-BAKE OVEN

scenes.text: The most exciting toy of all might have been a new bicycle. A Schwinn, with a bell, a basket and a headlight. Or a pair of metal roller skates, tightened onto your shoes with a skate key worn on a string around your neck. Kids skated for miles, and the clattering sound filled every sidewalk.
scenes.caption: THE SKATE KEY

scenes.text: And best of all, the Sears Christmas Wish Book, which arrived every fall. A ten-year-old studied it like a scholar. Every page was memorized. Every toy was circled. And every night, they dreamed about what might be under the tree on Christmas morning.
scenes.caption: THE WISH BOOK

scenes.text: Many ten-year-olds also joined the Cub Scouts, Brownies or Girl Scouts. They wore uniforms to school on meeting days, earned badges, sold cookies door to door, and went on camping trips where it always seemed to rain. The pinewood derby, where boys carved little race cars from blocks of wood with their fathers, was the highlight of the year.
scenes.caption: THE CUB SCOUTS

scenes.text: The fifth reason was school, believe it or not. Fourth and fifth grade in nineteen sixty-three meant reading Dick and Jane, practicing cursive with a fountain pen, and learning your times tables by heart. It meant milk breaks, recess, and a teacher who seemed a hundred years old but was probably forty.
scenes.caption: DICK AND JANE

scenes.text: At recess, kids played kickball, four square, tetherball and jump rope. Girls sang rhymes while they jumped. Boys traded baseball cards and argued about Mickey Mantle and Willie Mays. The playground had metal slides that got scorching hot in June, and merry-go-rounds that spun much too fast.
scenes.caption: RECESS

scenes.text: Lunch at school cost about a quarter, and it came on a tray with little compartments. Fish sticks, sloppy joes, pizza squares and canned peaches. Or kids brought a lunch box with a cartoon on it, and a thermos that usually leaked. Trading at the lunch table was serious business. A homemade cookie could buy almost anything.
scenes.caption: A QUARTER FOR LUNCH

scenes.text: And there were the school drills. Fire drills, and in nineteen sixty-three, still the occasional duck-and-cover drill. The Cuban Missile Crisis had happened just a year before, in October of sixty-two, and many ten-year-olds remembered how scared their parents had been. But most kids treated the drills like a game.
scenes.query: 1960s school children duck and cover drill
scenes.caption: DUCK AND COVER

scenes.text: The sixth reason was summer. School let out in early June, and summer seemed to last forever. There was the public swimming pool, with a deep end and a high diving board. There was Little League. There was summer camp, Vacation Bible School and long trips to see grandparents.
scenes.caption: SUMMER LASTED FOREVER

scenes.text: On summer nights, kids caught fireflies in mason jars with holes punched in the lid. They played kick the can, red rover and freeze tag until it was too dark to see. They chased the ice cream truck, and the mosquito fogger truck, which they should not have done. And they fell asleep exhausted, with the windows open.
scenes.caption: FIREFLIES IN A JAR

scenes.text: And in the summer of sixty-three, many towns held fairs and carnivals. Ferris wheels, cotton candy, the smell of popcorn and diesel from the rides. Kids rode the Tilt-A-Whirl until they felt sick, tried to win a goldfish by tossing a ping-pong ball into a bowl, and came home sunburned and happy.
scenes.caption: THE COUNTY FAIR

scenes.text: The seventh reason was music. In nineteen sixty-three, the radio was full of fun songs. The Beach Boys sang Surfin' U.S.A. Little Stevie Wonder, who was just thirteen, had a number one hit with Fingertips. There was It's My Party by Lesley Gore, and He's So Fine by the Chiffons.
scenes.caption: SURFIN' U.S.A.

scenes.text: And on the other side of the ocean, something was about to happen. In nineteen sixty-three, the Beatles were already the biggest thing in England. In December, I Want to Hold Your Hand came out in America. Within weeks, it was everywhere. By the time a ten-year-old turned eleven, the whole world had changed.
scenes.caption: I WANT TO HOLD YOUR HAND

scenes.text: The eighth reason was family. Most ten-year-olds in sixty-three sat down to dinner with their whole family every single night. Grandparents often lived nearby. Aunts, uncles and cousins came for Sunday dinner. Holidays were huge, loud and crowded, with a kids' table in the kitchen.
scenes.caption: THE KIDS' TABLE

scenes.text: Families took road trips together, in the station wagon, without seat belts or air conditioning. They stopped at roadside diners, motels with swimming pools, and tourist traps with signs for miles. Kids counted license plates and asked, over and over, how much longer.
scenes.caption: HOW MUCH LONGER?

scenes.text: At home, there were family rituals. Friday night was fish, or maybe a pizza from the new pizza place in town. Saturday night was baths and hair washing. Sunday was church, a big dinner and The Wonderful World of Color. These little routines gave kids a sense of order that many of them still miss.
scenes.caption: FAMILY RITUALS

scenes.text: The ninth reason was that a little money went a long way. A ten-year-old with an allowance of fifty cents a week was rich. A comic book cost twelve cents. A candy bar was a nickel. A bottle of Coke was a dime, and you got two cents back for the bottle. A movie matinee cost a quarter.
scenes.caption: A NICKEL CANDY BAR
scenes.chapter: 9. A dime went a long way

scenes.text: Kids earned money too. They collected soda bottles from ditches for the deposit. They mowed lawns, shoveled snow, sold lemonade and ran errands for neighbors. Many ten-year-olds had a savings account at the bank, with a little passbook where the teller stamped each deposit.
scenes.caption: THE LEMONADE STAND

scenes.text: And the tenth reason was innocence. In nineteen sixty-three, most ten-year-olds believed the world was a good place. Grown-ups were in charge, and they seemed to know what they were doing. The president was young, handsome and full of hope. America seemed like it could do anything.
scenes.caption: INNOCENCE

scenes.text: That innocence was shaken on November twenty-second, nineteen sixty-three. Many ten-year-olds were sitting in class when the principal's voice came over the loudspeaker. President Kennedy had been shot in Dallas. Teachers cried. Children were sent home early. For many, it was the first time they ever saw their fathers cry.
scenes.caption: NOVEMBER 22, 1963

scenes.text: For the next four days, the whole country watched television together. The funeral, the riderless horse, and three-year-old John Kennedy Junior saluting his father's casket. Many people say that weekend was the end of their childhood. They were ten, but they never quite felt that safe again.
scenes.caption: THE END OF CHILDHOOD

scenes.text: And yet, what most people remember about being ten in sixty-three isn't the sadness. It's the bikes, the fireflies, the cartoons, the astronauts and the long summer days. It's the feeling that the whole neighborhood was yours, and that there was always someone to play with.
scenes.caption: THE WHOLE NEIGHBORHOOD

scenes.text: If you were ten in nineteen sixty-three, you're in your early seventies today. You've seen the moon landing, the computer age and everything since. But I'd bet that if you close your eyes, you can still hear the screen door slam and your mother calling you home for dinner.
scenes.caption: THE SCREEN DOOR

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. How old were you in nineteen sixty-three, and where did you live? What was your favorite toy, your favorite show, or your favorite summer memory? We read every comment. Next time, we're asking what happened to the soda fountain. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: HOW OLD WERE YOU IN 1963?
